strengths: Introduces a genuinely useful benchmark, Moving Out, that bridges the gap between fully discrete grid-world collaboration testbeds (e.g., Overcooked-AI) and unconstrained/simplified continuous environments (e.g., It Takes Two), by grounding collaboration in a 2D physics engine with realistic constraints such as mass, shape, friction, and narrow passages.
The two proposed tasks (adapting to diverse human behavior; generalizing to unseen physical attributes) are well-motivated and map onto genuine challenges of embodied human-AI collaboration.

Substantial, carefully collected human-human interaction datasets (1,000+ demonstrations from 36 participants for Task 1; 720 expert demonstrations for Task 2), with IRB approval, add real value to the community beyond just an environment.

BASS combines two intuitive and technically reasonable ideas (sub-trajectory recombination for partner diversity, and a learned latent dynamics model for inference-time action selection) that are shown empirically to improve performance across multiple backbones (GRU, DP) and metrics.

Extensive empirical evaluation: AI-AI self-play comparisons, human-AI trials, a user study with statistically significant helpfulness/physics-understanding results, ablations isolating each BASS component, oracle-simulator upper-bound comparison, and qualitative failure-case analysis.

Strong reproducibility support via a large appendix detailing environment/observation encoding, hyperparameters, reward shaping for MAPPO, training compute, and additional cross-environment validation of BASS on Overcooked-AI, which supports generalizability claims.
weaknesses: Absolute performance numbers remain low across the board (TCR/NFD mostly in the 0.3-0.6 range even for the best method), indicating the benchmark and evaluated methods are far from solving the tasks; while this shows headroom, it also weakens the case that BASS constitutes a mature solution rather than an incremental improvement over weak baselines.

There is an unresolved inconsistency between the main text ("human subject study with 32 participants") and Appendix I ("12 volunteers"), which raises questions about which numbers back the reported statistics and undermines confidence in the reported human-study results.

Technical novelty is moderate: behavior augmentation via trajectory perturbation/recombination and action selection via a learned dynamics model are natural extensions of existing ideas (data augmentation, model-predictive action selection/world models) rather than fundamentally new mechanisms, and the paper's own related-work section cites several very similar prior approaches (Wang et al., Yuan et al., Ding et al.) without a rigorous, direct empirical comparison against them.

The comparison with MAPPO relies on an intricate, hand-engineered dense reward with numerous special-cased bonuses/penalties (Appendix C.2/Table 5), which could bias the RL baseline's performance either favorably or unfavorably and makes it hard to assess whether the RL vs. BC gap reflects an inherent limitation of RL or simply reward-design choices.

The sub-trajectory recombination technique depends on discretizing the continuous state space into a grid to find matching start/end poses (48x48 grid), which is a practical workaround that somewhat undercuts the paper's emphasis on the challenges of a truly continuous state space, and its scalability to larger/more complex maps or higher-dimensional embodiments is not discussed.

The environment, while physics-based, is still a simplified 2D top-down setting; the claims regarding "physically grounded" real-world collaboration (assembly, cooking, transport) are somewhat aspirational given the lack of 3D dynamics, contact-rich manipulation, or realistic robot embodiments.

No comparison against more recent zero-shot coordination methods explicitly designed for human-AI collaboration (e.g., population-based training variants, FCP, MEP) that are extensively cited in related work but never benchmarked, leaving open whether BASS's gains would hold against stronger, more specialized baselines.

strengths: Introduces a genuinely underexplored setting: continuous-space, physics-based human-AI collaboration, which contrasts with widely-used discrete grid-world benchmarks like Overcooked-AI and thus fills a real gap in the literature.

Non-trivial data collection effort: 1,000+ human-human demonstration pairs from 36 participants (Task 1) and 720 expert demonstrations (Task 2), collected under IRB approval, which could be a useful resource for future work.

The two-task design (adapting to diverse human behavior vs. generalizing to unseen physical attributes) is well-motivated and cleanly separates two distinct generalization challenges relevant to embodied collaboration.

Reasonably thorough empirical protocol: ablations isolating the augmentation and simulation/selection components of BASS, an oracle-simulator upper-bound comparison, a human subject study (32 participants) with a validated questionnaire and significance testing, and a qualitative failure-mode analysis.
Extensive appendix documentation (hyperparameters, reward design, environment/action encodings, map-by-map rationale) that aids reproducibility.
weaknesses: The environment is a 2D, CPU-only physics simulation built on a simplified game engine (Magical/Pymunk); calling this 'physically-grounded' robotics-relevant collaboration is a stretch compared to 3D embodied simulators, which limits the significance of claims about relevance to real-world robot-human collaboration.

Baselines are limited to generic behavior-cloning architectures (MLP, GRU, Diffusion Policy) and a single vanilla MAPPO; despite the related-work section extensively discussing zero-shot coordination methods that encourage behavioral diversity via self-play/population-based training (e.g., refs 15, 31, 33, 35, 36), none of these more appropriate and directly comparable baselines are evaluated, undermining the claim that BASS 'significantly outperforms state-of-the-art models.'

Reported results are noisy and not consistently favorable to BASS: in the full result tables (Appendix J), several BASS variants underperform their base models on specific metrics/tasks (e.g., MLP+BASS w/o Simulation drops TCR substantially in Task 2; mixed outcomes for GRU variants), yet the main text summarizes these as uniform improvements, and no significance tests are reported for the core AI-AI/human-AI task metrics (unlike the human questionnaire, which does report a t-test).

The 'Behavior Augmentation' technique stitches sub-trajectories from different human demonstrations based on coarse grid-cell matching of start/end poses; this could introduce physically inconsistent or non-causal partner transitions, and the paper's own admission that validity-checking is optional/unused raises concerns about training on potentially invalid data, with no quantitative analysis of how often stitched trajectories are physically implausible.

The core technical novelty of BASS is modest: it combines fairly standard trajectory-recombination augmentation with a sampling-based action selection scheme using a learned latent dynamics model (essentially short-horizon MPC/CEM with a world model) — a well-established idea in model-based RL/planning — rather than introducing a fundamentally new mechanism for human-AI physical collaboration.

MAPPO is reported to perform poorly, but the dense reward design (detailed in Appendix C) is hand-crafted and fairly specific to the benchmark; without stronger tuning or alternative RL baselines, it's unclear whether the comparison fairly represents RL's potential on this task, weakening the claim that BC+BASS is clearly superior to RL approaches.

The custom evaluation metrics (TCR, NFD, WT, AC) are benchmark-specific and not validated against or compared with established metrics from prior human-AI collaboration literature, which may hinder adoption and comparability by future work.

Sample sizes for both the physical-attribute dataset (4 expert players) and the human evaluation study (32 participants playing against only 2 methods, BASS vs. DP) are relatively small, limiting the statistical robustness and generalizability of the human-AI collaboration claims.

strengths: Introduces a well-motivated new benchmark (Moving Out) that fills a clear gap between discrete grid-world collaboration environments (Overcooked, LBF) and fully realistic 3D simulators (Habitat, HumanTHOR), by providing continuous-state 2D physics with diverse object shapes/sizes/masses that create meaningful physical constraints for collaboration.

Substantial, carefully designed data collection effort: over 1,000 human-human demonstrations from 36 participants for Task 1 and 720 expert demonstrations for Task 2, with IRB approval and clear collection protocols documented in the appendix.

The two proposed tasks (adapting to diverse human behavior vs. generalizing to unseen physical attributes) isolate distinct and important challenges for physically grounded collaboration, which is a thoughtful experimental design choice.

BASS is evaluated thoroughly: AI-AI self-play, human-AI user studies, ablations isolating augmentation vs. simulation components, comparison to an oracle physics simulator upper bound, and even a transfer check on Overcooked-AI showing the method is not narrowly tied to the proposed environment.

The paper includes a qualitative failure-case analysis and quantifies failure-mode reduction with BASS, which gives useful insight beyond aggregate metrics and supports the claimed benefits of the method.

Reproducibility materials are extensive: hyperparameters for all baselines (including MAPPO reward shaping details), architecture details for the dynamics model and autoencoders, and evaluation metric definitions are all specified in appendices.
weaknesses: There is an unresolved inconsistency in reported human-study sample sizes: Section 6.1 states the human subject study for RQ2 involved 32 participants, while Appendix I.1 states the questionnaire/model-selection study involved 12 volunteers; it is unclear whether these are the same or different studies, which undermines confidence in the reported human evaluation results and statistical claims (only one p-value, p=0.017, is reported for a single survey dimension).

The environment, while an improvement over grid-worlds, is still a simplified 2D physics simulation (built on Magical/Pymunk) with abstract circular/triangular agents and simple grasp mechanics; the term 'physically-grounded' may overstate the realism relative to actual robot embodiment, and the sim-to-real gap is not discussed beyond a brief mention in future work.

The core technical contribution (BASS) combines known ideas—trajectory/behavior augmentation and learned dynamics models for action scoring—that are explicitly acknowledged as similar to prior work (e.g., Wang et al., Yuan et al., Zhao et al.) in the related work section; the novelty lies mainly in the specific combination and application rather than a fundamentally new technique.

The data used for training is limited in participant diversity: only 4 expert players contributed all of the Task 2 demonstrations, which may not well represent a broad distribution of human strategies for the physical-generalization task despite the paper's claim of testing 'diverse human behavior.'

MAPPO's dense reward function required substantial map-specific hand-engineering (e.g., special handling for Map 11 grasp points, different gamma/entropy for coordination maps), making the RL baseline comparison potentially less representative of a well-tuned RL approach and raising concerns about fairness of baseline comparisons.

Some quantitative results show only modest or inconsistent gains from individual BASS components (e.g., Action Consistency improvements are small and sometimes within overlapping error bars in Tables 6-7), suggesting the practical significance of some claimed benefits could be more rigorously supported with significance testing across all metrics rather than just a single survey dimension.

strengths: Introduces a genuinely useful new benchmark (Moving Out) that fills a gap between symbolic/discrete human-AI collaboration environments (e.g., Overcooked-AI) and more complex but less physics-focused 3D simulators (Habitat 3.0, HumanTHOR); the environment incorporates continuous state-action spaces, object mass/shape/size variation, and physically-grounded constraints such as friction and narrow-passage navigation.

Substantial, carefully IRB-approved human data collection effort: >1,000 human-human demonstrations from 36 participants for Task 1 and 720 demonstrations from 4 experts for Task 2, with quantitative diversity analysis (DTW, entropy, coverage distance) showing the dataset is more diverse than expert- or RL-collected alternatives.

Two well-motivated evaluation tasks (adapting to unseen human behavior vs. generalizing to unseen physical attributes) with reproducible cross-group and compositional-generalization evaluation protocols that avoid the need to re-recruit humans for every test.

Extensive experimental validation: AI-AI comparisons against MLP/GRU/MAPPO/Diffusion Policy baselines, a human subject study (32 participants) with statistically significant results (p=0.017), qualitative failure case analysis, and a large appendix with many ablations (sampling strategy, module-wise accuracy, oracle-simulator upper bound, next-state predictor comparisons, BASS applied to Overcooked-AI).
Reasonably strong reproducibility documentation: detailed hyperparameters, observation/action encodings, reward shaping, and computing resource reporting are all provided in the appendix.
weaknesses: The core technical contribution (BASS) is largely a combination/adaptation of existing ideas—sub-trajectory stitching/augmentation (already used in single-agent offline RL) and learned dynamics models for model-based action selection—rather than a fundamentally new algorithmic idea; the paper itself acknowledges this lineage, which somewhat limits originality.

Baselines are relatively basic (MLP, GRU, vanilla Diffusion Policy, vanilla MAPPO); the paper does not compare against more competitive zero-shot-coordination methods discussed in its own related work (e.g., population-based training, FCP-style self-play with diverse partners, or generative-agent approaches), which would better contextualize how much BASS actually advances the state of the art in adapting to diverse humans.

Environment is 2D top-down physics (built on MAGICAL/Pymunk) rather than 3D or real-robot; while this is a reasonable simplification for tractable data collection, it somewhat limits the significance/generalizability of claims about "physically grounded" embodied collaboration relative to real-world robotic manipulation.

Human studies, while statistically significant, are based on modest sample sizes (32 participants for the main comparison, only 12 volunteers for the playing-with-models questionnaire study), and the self-report Likert-scale metrics (helpfulness, physics understanding, etc.) are not independently validated against behavioral ground truth beyond the paper's own correlational narrative.

Task 2's evaluation protocol (train on full dataset, evaluate via AI-AI self-play with novel attribute combinations) is a proxy that does not directly test generalization to unseen physical constraints with real humans, which is the more compelling test given the paper's motivation.

The real-time constraint (10Hz) limits the number of action candidates sampled for simulation-based selection to 4, and the ablation shows meaningfully better performance is available with more samples (4×4) at the cost of latency — this trade-off is acknowledged but not resolved, leaving the practical scalability of the simulate-and-select approach somewhat limited.

With only 12 hand-designed maps (across three collaboration modes), the diversity and difficulty scaling of the benchmark for broader community adoption is not fully demonstrated, despite claims of JSON-based extensibility.

strengths: Introduces a genuinely underexplored niche: a continuous, physics-based 2D human-AI collaboration benchmark that sits between symbolic Overcooked-style environments and heavy 3D simulators (Habitat, HumanTHOR), with explicit modeling of mass, shape, size and friction effects on collaboration.

Collected real human-human interaction data (1,000+ demonstrations from 36 participants for Task 1, 720 from 4 experts for Task 2) under IRB approval, and provides a quantitative diversity comparison (DTW, KDE entropy, coverage distance) showing the crowd-sourced data is more diverse than expert/RL-generated trajectories.
Proposes four complementary evaluation metrics (TCR, NFD, WT, AC) that attempt to capture different facets of physically grounded collaboration quality beyond simple task success.

Extensive appendix ablations (module-level accuracy of the dynamics model vs GRU/qVAE/random baselines, action-sampling strategy trade-offs, oracle-simulator upper bound, behavior augmentation validity checks) that, if integrated more concisely into the main text, would substantiate the design choices of BASS.

Conducts an actual human-subject study comparing BASS against a diffusion-policy baseline, including a Likert-scale questionnaire and qualitative failure-case analysis, which is a meaningful (if small-scale) step toward validating real human-AI usability.
weaknesses: Baseline comparison is narrow and somewhat weak: despite the related-work section citing numerous zero-shot-coordination and population-based training methods (FCP-style, diverse conventions, self-play variants), none are actually compared against; MAPPO is the only RL baseline and its reward function required substantial hand-engineering per Appendix F, raising doubts about whether it was competitively tuned, which could unfairly deflate the baseline and inflate BASS's relative gains.

The core evaluation protocols for "unseen human behavior" and "unseen physical constraints" are AI-AI proxies (splitting participants or self-play) rather than actual tests against new humans; while justified for reproducibility, this substantially weakens the central claim that the benchmark/method addresses adaptation to real diverse human behavior, since the proxy may not faithfully represent true human unpredictability.

Human-subject study details are inconsistent across the paper: the main text states 32 participants for the questionnaire-based comparison (Sec 6.1), while Appendix R separately reports a 12-volunteer study with different task framing (model selection, role switching) and compensation, making it unclear exactly how many humans contributed to which reported result and complicating reproducibility.

BASS's simulation/action-selection pipeline is heavily dependent on the partner action predictor, which only achieves ~71% accuracy at a 10% error tolerance; the ablation with randomized partner actions shows large performance degradation, suggesting the method's benefits may be fragile in more out-of-distribution or adversarial partner settings than tested.

Many standard errors reported in the appendix (e.g., Table 14/15/16) are large relative to the reported gains between DP and BASS, raising questions about the statistical robustness of several headline comparisons, especially under "unseen behavior" and Task 2 settings where differences are sometimes within one standard error of each other.

The underlying physics is a simplified 2D rigid-body engine (Magical-based), and the claimed "physically-grounded" and real-world relevance is not validated against any 3D or real robot setting, so generalizability of findings to actual embodied robot-human collaboration remains unclear.

Important architectural and implementation details of BASS (dynamics model structure, partner predictor design, augmentation validity guarantees) are deferred almost entirely to the appendix, making the main paper not self-contained and harder to assess methodological soundness without extensive cross-referencing.

The claim of being the "first benchmark with human-collected dataset designed to study continuous, low-level motion control" is a strong claim that is not rigorously substantiated against closely related continuous-action environments (e.g., Table Carrying, cited in their own comparison table).

strengths: Introduces a genuinely useful gap-filling benchmark: a 2D continuous-control, physics-based human-AI collaboration environment that sits between symbolic settings like Overcooked-AI and fully realistic but navigation-focused 3D simulators (Habitat 3.0, HumanTHOR). The taxonomy of collaboration modes (coordination, awareness, action consistency) is well motivated and the 12 maps are concretely illustrated with intuitive failure/success behaviors.

Substantial, IRB-approved human data collection effort: >1,000 human-human demonstrations from 36 participants for Task 1 and 720 expert demonstrations for Task 2, with a quantitative diversity analysis (DTW, KDE entropy, coverage distance) showing the dataset is more diverse than RL- or expert-generated data.

Thoughtful, reproducible evaluation protocols: rather than relying solely on live human trials (which are hard to reproduce), the authors design a cross-group AI-AI proxy evaluation for Task 1 and a held-out physical-attribute generalization protocol for Task 2, while still validating with an actual 32-participant human study.

BASS combines a multi-agent-aware trajectory augmentation technique (with explicit validity arguments for the start/end-state matching swap strategy) with a learned latent dynamics model for look-ahead action selection; the appendix provides extensive ablations (module-level accuracy, oracle-simulator comparison, GRU/qVAE alternatives, sampling-budget trade-offs) that support the design choices.

The human study includes both quantitative task metrics and a validated Likert-scale questionnaire with reported statistical significance (p=0.017) favoring BASS, and a qualitative failure-case analysis that is corroborated by participant feedback.
weaknesses: Despite the 'physically grounded' framing, the environment is a simplified 2D physics simulator (top-down, Magical/Pymunk-based); claims about addressing real-world embodied complexity (assembly, cooking, robots) are somewhat overstated relative to the actual testbed, which lacks 3D dynamics, visual perception, or realistic contact-rich manipulation.

Task 2's training data comes from only 4 expert players (720 demonstrations), which seems insufficient to capture diverse human adaptation strategies to physical variation, somewhat undermining the stated goal of studying how humans adapt to physical constraints at the same richness as Task 1.

The baseline comparisons are fairly standard (MLP, GRU, Diffusion Policy, MAPPO) and do not include more specialized zero-shot/human-aware coordination methods explicitly discussed in the related work (e.g., population-based training, FCP-style methods, diverse conventions), making it hard to judge how BASS compares against the actual state of the art in human-AI coordination rather than generic imitation/RL baselines.

The core technical novelty of BASS is incremental: trajectory recombination is a natural extension of existing stitching/augmentation ideas, and the action-selection mechanism is a simple best-of-N rollout scored by a learned one-step dynamics model (4 candidates for real-time constraints), which, while practical, is conceptually straightforward and whose benefits taper quickly (e.g., 2x2 sampling underperforms, 4x4 only marginally improves over 4x independent).

Next-state/partner-action prediction accuracy under Task 2 (unseen physical attributes) is modest (around 48.7% within 10% action-selection accuracy, and relatively lower prediction fidelity than Task 1), suggesting the dynamics model's understanding of novel physical constraints is still limited, somewhat weakening the generalization claims made for RQ2.

Many important clarifications (metric definitions, dynamics-model training details, data-collection logistics, map rationale) are relegated to a lengthy appendix, suggesting the main text alone may not be self-contained enough for assessing reproducibility without consulting substantial supplementary material.
